passage: Counsellor's note, Friday. Vijay, 21, a final-year student, came in after his father Wasim told him to accept the highest-paying job on offer, an office role he dreads. Vijay wants to become a school science teacher. He said, "Papa says a man has to earn well, and teaching won't do." I noted his flat voice and clenched hands. I asked if he would like me to meet his father with him. On Wednesday the three of us sat together. Wasim explained that he had struggled with money in his own youth and did not want that for his son. Vijay described the work he loves. Wasim asked what a teacher's first-year pay looks like and said he would think about it. I will see Vijay again next week.

qa.q: What job did Vijay's father want him to accept?
qa.a: Vijay's father wanted him to accept the highest-paying job on offer, an office role.

qa.q: What is Vijay feeling when he says "teaching won't do"?
qa.a: Vijay feels dismissed and tense. His flat voice and clenched hands suggest he is holding back frustration about being pushed into a mould.

qa.q: Which choice by Vijay opened the way to real family support?
qa.a: Vijay agreed to have the counsellor meet his father with him, so both could speak honestly and Wasim could hear the work Vijay loves.

qa.q: Why might Wasim have pushed for the highest-paying job?
qa.a: Wasim struggled with money in his own youth and did not want that for his son. His push comes from care, and he was willing to think again.

grounding: A young man is told to earn well rather than follow the work he loves, and real choice opens when his family listens with support.

passage: Tuesday night. Amma and Papa had a family talk at dinner. For me: "Take a government clerk job near home, Jahnavi. Easy hours, good for marriage." Amma says a daughter's job should be easy. For my brother Shankar: "Leave your art course, do engineering and earn well, or no girl will look at you." Shankar has not eaten his rice. We sat on the stairs afterwards and he said, "They're fitting both of us into moulds." I said I want to try the data analyst training in Hyderabad. He said he wants to paint and teach art. We agreed to ask Amma and Papa for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there. I'm nervous. But it's the first time either of us said what we really want out loud. Jahnavi

qa.q: What job did Amma and Papa suggest for Jahnavi?
qa.a: They suggested a government clerk job near home, with easy hours.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel about the conversation planned for Sunday?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels nervous but also relieved, because saying what she and Shankar really want out loud was a first.

qa.q: Which choice by Jahnavi and Shankar on the stairs could make real choice possible?
qa.a: They decided to say what each of them wants and to ask their parents for one honest conversation on Sunday, with Dadi there.

qa.q: How might Shankar see what their parents want for him?
qa.a: Shankar sees it as a mould. He is expected to leave his art course, do engineering and earn well, and he was too upset to eat his rice.

grounding: A young woman is told to pick an easy job for marriage while her brother is told to earn well, and they decide to ask their family for an honest talk.

passage:
Dear Santosh Bhaiya,
Congratulations on your placement. Papa has told the whole colony. Now he's telling me to do B.Ed. because "teaching is good for marriage, only half day."
I'm writing because I think you'll understand. You wanted to study history. Papa said engineering pays, and now you have the job everyone praises, and you told me last Diwali that you hate the code.
They've put both of us in boxes. You're meant to earn big. I'm meant to earn small and be home by four.
I want to do my master's in public health. I've found the course. I'm going to tell Papa and Mummy this Sunday. Will you sit with me? If they hear it from both of us, that our choices shouldn't depend on whether we're a son or a daughter, maybe they'll listen.
Your sister,
Payal

qa.q: What is Papa telling Payal to do?
qa.a: Papa is telling Payal to do B.Ed. because teaching is good for marriage, only half day.

qa.q: How does Payal feel about the boxes she and her brother are put in?
qa.a: Payal feels frustrated and boxed in, and also hopeful that Santosh will understand, since he was pushed into engineering too.

qa.q: Why is asking Santosh to sit with her a good step?
qa.a: Two siblings showing that both were fitted into moulds can help their parents see the pattern and support each child's own choice.

qa.q: What is it like for Santosh to have the job everyone praises?
qa.a: Santosh has success others admire, but he told Payal he hates the code, so he may feel trapped and unhappy despite the praise.

grounding: A young woman writes to her brother about both being fitted into gendered career moulds, and plans to seek real choice with family support.

passage:
Pradeep, you know me as the guy who quit engineering. Here's what really happened.
Everyone in my family said the same thing: "You're the son. You have to earn well." My cousin sister was told to take a bank job, simple and safe, because she'd marry. Nobody asked either of us what we liked.
I liked caring for people. When Nani was in hospital, I stayed three nights and the nurses said I had steady hands. I wanted to be a nurse. I said it once at dinner and my uncle laughed so hard he coughed.
For a year I did engineering and felt nothing. Then I sat with my mother alone and told her. She was quiet. Then she said, "You held my mother's hand better than any of us." She talked to Papa for me.
So now I'm in nursing college. That's me, Chetan, and that's the whole story.

qa.q: What did the nurses say Chetan had?
qa.a: The nurses said Chetan had steady hands.

qa.q: What did Chetan feel during the year of engineering?
qa.a: Chetan felt nothing, empty and stuck in a path chosen for him because he was the son.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and why did it work?
qa.a: Chetan spoke to his mother alone; she remembered him caring for Nani and then spoke to Papa, so family support opened the way for his real choice.

qa.q: How might Chetan's cousin sister see her own path after hearing his story?
qa.a: She might feel encouraged to question the safe bank job she was told to take and ask what she herself wants.

grounding: A young man pushed to earn well and a young woman pushed toward an easy job are both fitted into moulds, and family support makes real choice possible.

passage:
Monday. At dinner, Amma told Keerthana, twenty, to apply for the simple office job at the cooperative, "something that won't trouble your in-laws." In the same breath she told Ujjwal, her twin, to take the high-paying sales job in Chennai, "because a man must provide." Neither twin said a word.
Thursday. On the terrace, Keerthana admitted she wanted to train as a pilot. Ujjwal laughed, then stopped. "I want to stay here and run a bakery." They stared at each other and burst out laughing.
Sunday. They sat down with Amma and Appa together. Keerthana showed the flying academy brochure; Ujjwal showed his baking notebook. Appa was silent for a long time. Then he said, "Both of you, show me a plan. Real numbers. We'll look at it together." Amma looked worried, but she nodded.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say he wanted to run?
qa.a: Ujjwal said he wanted to stay here and run a bakery.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana and Ujjwal burst out laughing on the terrace?
qa.a: They were relieved and surprised to find that both of them wanted something different from what they'd been told, and felt less alone.

qa.q: What made the Sunday talk work?
qa.a: They spoke together and brought something concrete, a brochure and a notebook, so their parents could see real plans instead of just objections.

qa.q: How might Amma feel when she nods?
qa.a: Amma probably feels worried about the unusual paths but also willing to support them, torn between her fears and her children's wishes.

grounding: Over three days, twins told a daughter should take an easy job for marriage and a son must earn well find their real choices with family support.

passage:
Vijay, your father wants you to be an engineer, and you want to cook? Let your Gargi athai tell you something. When I was twenty, I had topped my college in chemistry. My father said, "Do a B.Ed. Teaching is a good job for a girl. Easy hours, good for marriage." My twin brother, your father, wanted to paint. He was told, "Painting? You must earn. You're the son." So I became a teacher and he became an engineer. Both of us were pushed into moulds, one for a wedding, one for a salary.
The turning point came years later, when I told my father I wanted to do research after all. My mother, who had never spoken against him, said, "Let her." That changed everything. I got my PhD at thirty-two. Your father still paints on Sundays. Beta, talk to him. He knows that mould better than anyone.

qa.q: What did Gargi's father tell her to do after college?
qa.a: To do a B.Ed., because teaching was a good job for a girl.

qa.q: How might young Gargi have felt when told to choose teaching for marriage?
qa.a: She probably felt disappointed and boxed in, having topped her college in chemistry.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Her mother saying "Let her" when Gargi asked to do research; family support finally made a real choice possible.

qa.q: How might Gargi's twin brother have felt being told he must earn?
qa.a: He probably felt trapped and sad, giving up painting for engineering, which is why he still paints on Sundays.

grounding: It illustrates a young woman steered to an easy job for marriage while her brother is told to earn, and how real choice came with family support.
